metadata.description: Enhanced Node.js Interview Questions - Deep theoretical explanations for 3.5+ years backend experience
metadata.usage: Merge with nodeJs.js via nodeQuestionsMerged.js or import directly

enhancedQuestions.question: What is Node.js? - Deep dive into architecture and design decisions
enhancedQuestions.answer: Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform runtime environment that executes JavaScript outside the browser. But that definition is surface-level. Here's the senior-level understanding: Architecture (The How): - V8 Engine: Node.js embeds Google's V8—Chrome's JavaScript engine. V8 compiles JS to native machine code (JIT compilation), making it fast. It also provides the event loop model at the language level. - libuv: A C library that provides the actual event loop implementation. While V8 handles JS execution, libuv handles I/O (file system, network, timers) and the thread pool. Think of it as the "operating system" for Node's async model. - Node Bindings: C++ glue code that connects V8, libuv, and Node's JavaScript APIs (fs, http, etc.). Why Event-Driven, Non-Blocking I/O? Web servers spend most of their time waiting—for database queries, file reads, external APIs. Traditional blocking I/O would tie one thread per connection. With 10,000 connections, you'd need 10,000 threads (massive memory: ~1MB stack per thread). Node's model uses a single thread + non-blocking I/O: when a DB query is pending, the thread handles other requests. When the query completes, a callback runs. This scales to millions of connections with minimal memory. Real-World Use Cases: APIs, microservices, real-time apps (chat, gaming), stream processing, BFF (Backend-for-Frontend) layers. Common Pitfall: Node.js excels at I/O-bound work. CPU-intensive tasks (image processing, cryptographic hashing, JSON parsing of huge payloads) block the event loop and hurt all concurrent requests. Use Worker Threads or external processes for those.

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain the Event Loop in Node.js - All phases and internal mechanism
enhancedQuestions.answer: The Event Loop is the heart of Node's non-blocking model. It's a single-threaded loop that continuously checks for work and executes callbacks. Here's the full picture. Phases (in order): 1. Timers: Runs setTimeout/setInterval callbacks. Note: setTimeout(fn, 0) does NOT run immediately—it queues for the next timers phase. 2. Pending callbacks: Executes I/O callbacks deferred from the previous cycle (e.g., TCP errors). 3. Idle, Prepare: Internal use only (libuv housekeeping). 4. Poll: Most important phase. Retrieves new I/O events; executes I/O callbacks (file reads, HTTP responses). If the queue is empty, it may block here waiting for events (with a timeout based on the next timer). 5. Check: Runs setImmediate() callbacks. 6. Close callbacks: Runs close events (e.g., socket.on('close')). Between each phase: Node runs process.nextTick queue, then microtasks (Promise callbacks). So: nextTick runs before microtasks, and both run between phases. Why this order matters: - setImmediate vs setTimeout(0): In the main module, their order can vary; inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before setTimeout because it's in the Check phase (after Poll). - process.nextTick: Bypasses the event loop phases. It runs after the current JS stack clears, before the next phase. Overuse can starve the event loop ("nextTick starvation"). Plain-language terms: - Event loop: A loop that repeatedly asks "Is there a callback ready?" and runs it. - Phase: A stage in that loop that handles a specific type of callback (timers, I/O, etc.).

enhancedQuestions.question: What is libuv and how does it relate to Node.js architecture?
enhancedQuestions.answer: libuv is a cross-platform C library that provides asynchronous I/O to Node.js. It's not part of Node.js—it's a dependency that Node wraps. Understanding it is crucial for senior backend roles. What libuv provides: 1. Event Loop: The actual loop implementation. Node's JS layer sits on top; when you call fs.readFile, Node passes the work to libuv, which runs the loop and notifies Node when the file is read. 2. Thread Pool: By default, libuv creates 4 worker threads (configurable via UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE). Operations that cannot be truly async at the OS level (e.g., fs operations, DNS lookups, crypto.pbkdf2, zlib) are offloaded here. The OS doesn't offer async file I/O on all platforms, so libuv uses threads. 3. Abstracts OS differences: epoll (Linux), kqueue (macOS), IOCP (Windows). Your Node code works the same everywhere. Which operations use the thread pool? - fs (file system) - most methods - dns.lookup() (not dns.resolve—that uses libuv's async resolver) - crypto (pbkdf2, randomBytes, etc.) - zlib Which operations bypass the thread pool? - Network I/O (sockets, HTTP): Uses OS-level async I/O (epoll/kqueue/IOCP). - Timers: Handled in the event loop. Performance implication: If you run 5 crypto.pbkdf2 calls concurrently with the default pool of 4, the 5th waits. Increase UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE for workloads heavy on file/crypto. Too high can cause thread contention.

enhancedQuestions.question: Microtask vs Macrotask queue - Execution order and implications
enhancedQuestions.answer: Node.js (and browsers) have two types of task queues that affect when your callbacks run. Getting this wrong causes subtle bugs. Macrotasks (Task Queue): - What: setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate, I/O callbacks. These are scheduled in the event loop phases. - When: One macrotask per phase; after it runs, microtasks are flushed before the next macrotask. Microtasks (Microtask Queue): - What: Promise callbacks (.then, .catch, .finally), queueMicrotask(), MutationObserver (browser). - When: Run after the current macrotask completes, before the next macrotask. All microtasks in the queue run until it's empty (can cause starvation if you schedule many). process.nextTick: Not in either queue. It has its own queue and runs after the current operation, before microtasks. Highest priority. Order (conceptual): 1. Run one macrotask (e.g., a setTimeout callback) 2. Run all process.nextTick callbacks 3. Run all microtasks (Promises) 4. Repeat for next macrotask Real-world pitfall: A long promise chain (e.g., 1000 .then callbacks) will block the event loop because microtasks run to completion. The next setTimeout won't run until all 1000 complete. Same with recursive process.nextTick—avoid it.

enhancedQuestions.question: setImmediate vs process.nextTick vs setTimeout(fn, 0) - When to use each
enhancedQuestions.answer: All three defer execution, but at different points in the event loop. Choosing wrong can cause ordering bugs or performance issues. process.nextTick(callback): - When it runs: After the current operation, before the event loop continues. It's not part of any event loop phase—it inserts at the "earliest possible" moment. - Use case: Defer a callback to allow the current stack to unwind (e.g., in an API that accepts a callback—call it "asynchronously" but as soon as possible). - Pitfall: Recursive nextTick blocks the event loop. Never do: function tick() { process.nextTick(tick); } setImmediate(callback): - When it runs: In the Check phase, after the Poll phase. So it runs after I/O callbacks. - Use case: "Run this after the current event loop iteration"—e.g., after handling all I/O. Good for breaking up long-running work. - Note: Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate runs before setTimeout(0) because Check comes before the next Timers phase. setTimeout(fn, 0): - When it runs: In the Timers phase. Minimum delay is ~1–4ms (browser/Node clamp it). - Use case: "Run after a short delay" or when you want to yield to I/O. Less precise than setImmediate for "after current tick" semantics. Recommendation: Prefer setImmediate over setTimeout(0) for "run after current operations." Use nextTick only when you need to defer to "before the next phase" (rare).

enhancedQuestions.question: Explain Streams in Node.js - Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform with backpressure
enhancedQuestions.answer: Streams are abstractions for handling data in chunks rather than loading everything into memory. Essential for large files, HTTP bodies, and real-time data. Types: 1. Readable: Data source (fs.createReadStream, HTTP request body, process.stdin). You consume with .on('data') or .pipe(). 2. Writable: Data sink (fs.createWriteStream, HTTP response, process.stdout). You write with .write() and signal end with .end(). 3. Duplex: Both read and write (TCP sockets, WebSockets). Two independent streams. 4. Transform: Duplex that modifies data (zlib.createGzip, crypto streams). Input flows in, transformed output flows out. Backpressure (Critical for production): When the consumer is slower than the producer, data backs up. Without backpressure, memory grows until OOM. Streams handle this: - Writable returns false from .write() when its buffer is full—stop writing until 'drain' event. - .pipe() handles this automatically between streams. - Manual handling: if (!writable.write(chunk)) readable.pause(); writable.once('drain', () => readable.resume()); Real-world: Proxy large uploads, log aggregation, video transcoding, CSV parsing. Never use fs.readFile for multi-GB files—use streams. Pitfall: Piping to a slow destination without handling backpressure causes memory spikes. Always use .pipe() or implement drain logic.

enhancedQuestions.question: Worker Threads vs Cluster module - When to use which?
enhancedQuestions.answer: Both enable parallelism, but for different problems. Cluster: - What: Multiple Node.js processes, each with its own V8 instance and memory. Shares a port via the master process. - Use case: Scaling I/O-bound servers (HTTP, WebSocket). One process per CPU core handles requests independently. If one crashes, others continue. - Communication: IPC (process.send, message events). Serialization overhead. - Memory: Each process has full heap. 4 cores = 4x baseline memory. Worker Threads: - What: Threads within a single process. Share the process but have isolated V8 contexts. Can share memory via SharedArrayBuffer. - Use case: CPU-intensive work (image processing, heavy computations, parsing large JSON) without blocking the main thread. - Communication: postMessage or SharedArrayBuffer (zero-copy for large data). - Memory: Lighter than processes; shared memory reduces duplication. Decision tree: - Need to scale HTTP server? → Cluster (or use PM2 which uses cluster under the hood). - Need to run CPU-heavy logic without blocking? → Worker Threads. - Need fault isolation (crash one worker, others survive)? → Cluster.

enhancedQuestions.question: How does Node.js handle garbage collection? What should backend developers know?
enhancedQuestions.answer: Node uses V8's garbage collector. Understanding it helps avoid memory leaks and long GC pauses. Two main collectors: 1. Minor GC (Scavenger): Runs on the "new space" (young objects). Fast, runs frequently. Objects that survive copy to "old space." 2. Major GC (Mark-Sweep-Compact): Runs on the "old space." Slower; can cause 10–100ms+ pauses. Compacts memory to reduce fragmentation. Heap structure (plain terms): - New space: Short-lived objects (e.g., per-request data). Collected often. - Old space: Long-lived objects. Collected less often. - Large object space: Objects too big for other spaces (e.g., buffers > ~2MB). Implications for backends: - Avoid storing request-scoped data in global/module-level variables (e.g., caches that grow unbounded). - Large buffers (e.g., Buffer.alloc(50 * 1024 * 1024)) go to large object space—GC treats them differently. - Long GC pauses block the event loop. Monitor with --expose-gc and gc stats. Consider --max-old-space-size if you have enough RAM. Memory leak patterns: Global arrays/maps that accumulate, unclosed timers/listeners, closures holding references to large objects.
enhancedQuestions.codeExample:
// Inspect heap: node --expose-gc --max-old-space-size=4096 app.js
// In code: global.gc() to force GC (for testing)

enhancedQuestions.question: What is the Process object and what critical properties/methods does it provide?
enhancedQuestions.answer: process is a global object providing information about and control over the current Node.js process. Backend developers use it daily. Key properties: - process.env: Environment variables. Use for config (NODE_ENV, DATABASE_URL). Never commit secrets here—use .env files loaded by dotenv. - process.argv: Command-line args. process.argv[0]=node, [1]=script path, [2]+=your args. - process.pid: Process ID. - process.cwd(): Current working directory. Can change with process.chdir(). - process.memoryUsage(): { rss, heapTotal, heapUsed, external }. Useful for monitoring. - process.versions: Node, V8, libuv, etc. Signals and shutdown: - process.on('SIGTERM', ...): Graceful shutdown. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM before SIGKILL. Close DB connections, finish in-flight requests, then process.exit(0). - process.on('SIGINT', ...): Ctrl+C. - process.exit(code): 0=success, non-zero=failure. Avoid in libraries—let the process exit naturally. Uncaught handling: - process.on('uncaughtException', ...): Last resort. Log, alert, then exit. Don't try to "recover"—state may be corrupted. - process.on('unhandledRejection', ...): Unhandled promise rejections. Log and consider exiting in production. Best practice: Use a shutdown wrapper (e.g., Promise-based) that sets a "shutting down" flag, stops accepting new work, waits for in-flight requests (with timeout), then exits.

enhancedQuestions.question: Buffer vs Stream - When to use which and memory implications
enhancedQuestions.answer: Both handle data, but at different granularities. Buffer: - What: Fixed-size chunk of raw bytes in memory. Like a byte array. Lives in V8's heap or off-heap (depending on size). - Use case: When you need to hold a discrete chunk (e.g., file read into memory, cryptographic input, protocol framing). For small to medium data. - Pitfall: Loading a 1GB file into a buffer allocates 1GB. Can cause OOM or major GC pressure. Stream: - What: Abstraction for data that arrives/leaves in chunks over time. No single "buffer" holding everything. - Use case: Large files, HTTP request/response bodies, real-time data, piping. Memory stays bounded (chunk size, e.g., 64KB). - Relationship: Each stream chunk is often a Buffer. Streams are the "pipe," buffers are the "water" flowing through. Decision: If the entire dataset fits comfortably in memory (e.g., < 10MB) and you need random access, Buffer/readFile is fine. If it's large or unbounded, use streams.

newQuestions.question: Explain libuv architecture - Event loop, thread pool, and OS abstraction
newQuestions.answer: libuv is the C library that powers Node's async I/O. It has two main components: 1. Event Loop: A single-threaded loop. Each iteration ("tick") runs: timers → pending callbacks → idle/prepare → poll (I/O) → check (setImmediate) → close. Between phases, nextTick and microtasks run. The poll phase can block waiting for I/O (with a timeout). 2. Thread Pool: Default 4 threads. Used when the OS doesn't provide async APIs: file system, dns.lookup, crypto (pbkdf2, scrypt), zlib. Network I/O uses OS mechanisms (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) and bypasses the pool. 3. OS Abstraction: epoll (Linux), kqueue (macOS/BSD), IOCP (Windows). libuv translates Node's fs/net APIs into the right syscalls per platform. Performance: UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE caps concurrent fs/crypto work. For crypto-heavy apps, increase it (e.g., 16).
newQuestions.codeExample: process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE = 16; // Must set before any async work

newQuestions.question: How do you avoid blocking the event loop? What operations are dangerous?
newQuestions.answer: Blocking = synchronous work that keeps the main thread busy so it can't process I/O or timers. Users see latency; under load, the server stalls. Dangerous operations: - Synchronous fs: readFileSync, writeFileSync, existsSync. Use async versions. - CPU-heavy JS: Large JSON.parse/stringify, complex regex, tight loops (e.g., crypto in JS). - Native modules that block: Some npm packages use sync C++ calls. Solutions: 1. Use async APIs (fs.promises, non-blocking network). 2. Offload CPU work to Worker Threads or child processes. 3. Partition work: Break large tasks into chunks, yield with setImmediate between chunks. 4. Avoid regex on unbounded input (ReDoS); use safe parsers. 5. Monitor: Use --trace-sync-io to find sync I/O, or measure event loop delay with perf hooks. Event loop delay: If delay > 100ms, you're blocking. Tools: clinic.js, 0x, Node's perf hooks.

newQuestions.question: Explain Child Processes - spawn, exec, execFile, fork. When to use each?
newQuestions.answer: child_process creates separate processes. Different methods for different needs. spawn(command, args, options): - Launches a process, returns ChildProcess with stdin/stdout/stderr streams. No shell by default. Best for long-running processes (e.g., ffmpeg, scripts). Use when you need streaming I/O. exec(command, callback): - Runs command in a shell. Buffers stdout/stderr and returns when process exits. Max buffer default 1MB. Use for short commands where you need the full output. Risk: shell injection if command is user input. execFile(file, args, callback): - Like exec but no shell—direct execution. Safer for user input. Can't use shell features (pipes, redirects). fork(modulePath, args, options): - Specialized spawn for Node. Runs another Node script. Sets up IPC channel (process.send, 'message' event). Used by Cluster. Best for Node-to-Node multiprocessing. Use cases: spawn for CLI tools; exec for one-off shell commands; execFile when you need safety; fork for Node workers.

How would you implement rate limiting in a Node.js API?
newQuestions.answer: Rate limiting restricts how many requests a client can make in a time window. Prevents abuse and protects downstream services. Approaches: 1. In-memory (e.g., sliding window counter): Store request counts per key (IP, user ID) in a Map. Increment on request; reject if over limit. Simple but doesn't work across multiple instances (each has its own memory). 2. Redis: INCR + EXPIRE, or sliding window log. Works across instances. Standard for production. 3. Token bucket / Leaky bucket: More smooth rate. Tokens replenish over time; each request consumes a token. Identify the client: IP, API key, user ID. IP can be spoofed (X-Forwarded-For); use authenticated identity when possible. Response: 429 Too Many Requests. Include Retry-After header. Use middleware (e.g., express-rate-limit) for consistency. Real-world: Different limits per endpoint (auth: 5/min, search: 100/min). Tiered by plan. Combine with circuit breakers for downstream protection.

newQuestions.question: Explain horizontal vs vertical scaling for Node.js backends
newQuestions.answer: Vertical scaling: Add more CPU/RAM to one machine. Simpler (one process, one DB connection pool) but hits hardware limits. Cost grows non-linearly. Single point of failure. Horizontal scaling: Add more machines (instances). Each runs Node; load balancer distributes traffic. Scales to many instances. Requires stateless app design—sessions in Redis, not memory. Database becomes bottleneck; use read replicas, connection pooling, caching. Node-specific: Node is single-threaded per process. One process uses one core. To use all cores on a machine: Cluster module or process managers (PM2). For multi-machine: Kubernetes, ECS, or VM fleet behind a load balancer. When to choose: Start vertical for simplicity; go horizontal when you need more throughput or HA. Cloud: prefer horizontal (auto-scaling groups).

newQuestions.question: How do you implement graceful shutdown in a Node.js server?
newQuestions.answer: Graceful shutdown = stop accepting new requests, finish in-flight ones, close DB/Redis, then exit. Essential for zero-downtime deploys and clean restarts. Steps: 1. Listen for SIGTERM (and SIGINT for Ctrl+C). 2. Set a "shutting down" flag; stop accepting new connections (server.close()). 3. Wait for active requests to complete (track with a counter or timeout). 4. Close DB pool, Redis, message queue consumers. 5. process.exit(0). Timeout: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits (terminationGracePeriodSeconds, default 30s), then SIGKILL. Finish within that window or force exit. Pitfalls: Not calling server.close() leaves connections hanging. Exiting before DB closes can corrupt state. Use a shutdown helper (e.g., terminus, custom) to orchestrate.

newQuestions.question: How do you prevent XSS and CSRF in a Node.js/Express API?
newQuestions.answer: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): Attacker injects script into pages. For APIs, risk is lower (APIs return JSON, not HTML), but if you render user input in HTML (e.g., SSR), escape output. Use a templating engine with auto-escaping (EJS, Pug). Set Content-Type correctly. Content-Security-Policy header restricts script sources. CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): Attacker tricks a logged-in user's browser into making requests to your API. Mitigations: 1. SameSite cookies (SameSite=Strict or Lax). 2. CSRF tokens: Server generates token, client sends in header or body. Validate on state-changing requests. 3. Custom headers (e.g., X-Requested-With) that browser doesn't send cross-origin. Not foolproof but adds friction. 4. For APIs: Use tokens (JWT in Authorization header) instead of cookies for auth—CORS prevents cross-origin sends. If using cookie-based sessions, combine with CSRF tokens. Summary: XSS: escape output, CSP. CSRF: SameSite, tokens, or token-based auth.

newQuestions.question: What is Helmet and how do secure headers protect your API?
newQuestions.answer: Helmet is a middleware that sets security-related HTTP headers. It's a collection of smaller middlewares, each setting one or more headers. Key headers Helmet sets: - Content-Security-Policy (CSP): Restricts where scripts, styles, and resources can load from. Mitigates XSS. - X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — Prevents MIME sniffing. Forces browser to respect Content-Type. - X-Frame-Options: DENY or SAMEORIGIN — Prevents clickjacking (embedding your site in iframe). - Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS): Tells browser to use HTTPS only. - X-XSS-Protection: Legacy XSS filter (mostly obsolete but harmless). Usage: app.use(helmet()). Customize with options if defaults break your app (e.g., CSP can block inline scripts). API-specific: For JSON APIs, CSP is less critical. HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, and X-Frame-Options still help. Disable defaults that interfere (e.g., contentSecurityPolicy: false) if needed.

newQuestions.question: How do you manage environment variables and secrets in Node.js?
newQuestions.answer: Environment variables: process.env. Use for config that varies by environment (NODE_ENV, PORT, DATABASE_URL). Never commit secrets. Loading: dotenv loads .env into process.env. Call require('dotenv').config() at app startup. Use different files (.env.development, .env.production) or inject via CI/CD. Secrets best practices: 1. Never hardcode. Use env vars or a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault). 2. .env in .gitignore. Provide .env.example with placeholder keys (no values). 3. Validate required vars at startup: if (!process.env.DATABASE_URL) throw new Error('DATABASE_URL required'). 4. In production, inject via container orchestrator (Kubernetes secrets, ECS task definitions) or deployment pipeline. Type coercion: process.env returns strings. Parse numbers (parseInt) or booleans explicitly.

newQuestions.question: JWT vs Session-based authentication - Pros, cons, and when to use each
newQuestions.answer: Session-based: Server stores session (in memory or Redis). Client gets session ID in cookie. Server looks up session on each request. Pros: Easy to invalidate (delete session). Cons: Server state; scaling requires shared store (Redis). JWT (JSON Web Token): Stateless. Server signs a payload (e.g., userId, exp), client stores token (cookie or Authorization header). Server verifies signature, no DB lookup. Pros: Stateless, works across services. Cons: Hard to invalidate before expiry (need blocklist or short TTL). Token size larger than session ID. When to use: Sessions for traditional web apps with logout/invalidate needs. JWT for APIs, microservices, mobile apps, when you want stateless auth. Security: Store JWT in httpOnly cookie to reduce XSS theft, or in memory for SPAs. Use HTTPS. Short expiry (15min) + refresh token for long-lived access. Validate signature, exp, issuer.

newQuestions.question: How would you design a scalable REST API in Node.js?
newQuestions.answer: Structure: Layered: routes → controllers → services → repositories. Keep routes thin; business logic in services; data access in repositories. Stateless: No in-memory session. Use JWT or external session store. Any instance can handle any request. Idempotency: For POST/PUT, support Idempotency-Key header. Store result by key; return same response for duplicate requests. Pagination: Cursor-based for large datasets (more stable than offset). Return next_cursor, limit. Versioning: URL (/v1/users) or header (Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=1). Rate limiting: Per client (IP or API key). 429 with Retry-After. Health checks: /health (liveness), /ready (readiness: DB, Redis up). Kubernetes uses these for probes. Logging: Structured JSON. Request ID for tracing. Correlation ID across services. Caching: Cache-Control, ETag for GET. Redis for frequent reads.

newQuestions.question: What caching strategies can you use in a Node.js backend?
newQuestions.answer: 1. In-memory (e.g., node-cache, lru-cache): Fast, per-process. Lost on restart. Good for small, non-critical data (e.g., config). Not shared across instances. 2. Redis: Shared across instances. TTL support. Use for sessions, rate limiting, API response cache. Pattern: Check cache → miss → fetch from DB → set cache → return. 3. HTTP caching: Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified. Browser/CDN caches. For public GET endpoints. Reduces server load. 4. Cache-aside: App manages cache. On read: check cache; on miss, load from DB and populate cache. On write: update DB, invalidate or update cache. 5. Write-through: Write to cache and DB together. Cache is always fresh but writes are slower. 6. Stale-while-revalidate: Return stale cache immediately, revalidate in background. Good for high read, acceptable staleness. Invalidation: Hardest part. TTL is simple. Explicit invalidation on writes requires knowing keys. Use cache tags or version keys for related data.

newQuestions.question: How do you implement input validation in a Node.js API?
newQuestions.answer: Always validate and sanitize input. Use a schema library (Joi, Zod, Yup) or express-validator. Why: Prevents injection (SQL, NoSQL, command), type errors, and malformed data. Fail fast with 400 Bad Request. Where: At the edge—in middleware or at controller entry. Validate body, query, params, headers. Approach: Define schema (e.g., Joi.object({ email: Joi.string().email(), age: Joi.number().min(0) })). Validate request; if invalid, return 400 with error details. Use sanitization (escape HTML, trim) where applicable. Common pitfalls: Only validating on client; accepting arrays/objects without size limits (DoS); not validating nested structures. Use max length on strings and arrays. SQL injection: Use parameterized queries (prepared statements). Never concatenate user input into SQL. NoSQL injection: Validate types. Don't pass user objects directly to Mongoose find({ ...req.body }).

newQuestions.question: How do you detect and fix memory leaks in Node.js?
newQuestions.answer: Signs: Heap grows over time, doesn't drop after GC. OOM crashes. High RSS. Tools: node --inspect + Chrome DevTools (Memory tab, take heap snapshot, compare). clinic.js for production profiling. 0x for flamegraphs. Common causes: 1. Global variables accumulating (arrays, maps, caches without TTL or max size). 2. Closures holding references (e.g., in event listeners that are never removed). 3. Timers (setInterval) never cleared. 4. Detached DOM (browser) or similar—less common in Node. Fixes: Limit cache size (LRU). Remove listeners (EventEmitter.off). Clear intervals. Avoid storing request-scoped data in module scope. Use WeakMap for caches where keys are objects and you're okay with GC reclaiming. Process: Reproduce leak (load test), take heap snapshots before and after, compare retained size, find growing objects, trace to source.

newQuestions.question: What is the Reactor Pattern and how does Node.js use it?
newQuestions.answer: The Reactor Pattern is a design for handling multiple I/O sources with a single thread. It's event-driven: when I/O is ready, a handler runs. Components: 1. Demultiplexer (synchronous event multiplexer): OS primitive (select, poll, epoll, kqueue). Blocks until one or more I/O operations are ready. 2. Event loop: Loops: call demultiplexer → get ready handles → dispatch to handlers. 3. Handlers: Callbacks associated with each I/O handle. Run when the handle is ready. Node's implementation: libuv provides the demultiplexer and event loop. When you do fs.readFile, Node registers the file handle with libuv. libuv uses epoll/kqueue. When the read completes, libuv queues the callback; the event loop runs it. Why it works: One thread handles many I/O operations. While one is waiting (e.g., network), others can complete. No thread-per-connection overhead.

newQuestions.question: How does the Cluster module load balance requests?
newQuestions.answer: The cluster module creates multiple worker processes. All workers listen on the same port. The OS kernel distributes incoming connections across the listening sockets ( round-robin on most platforms). Flow: Master creates a server socket, binds to port. Workers are forked. Master passes the socket to workers (or they inherit). When a connection arrives, the kernel hands it to one worker. Which worker is platform-dependent (Linux: round-robin; Windows: different). Note: Cluster doesn't do application-level load balancing (e.g., by URL or cookie). It's connection-level. For HTTP, one TCP connection can have multiple requests (HTTP/1.1 keep-alive). The same worker handles all requests on that connection. Session stickiness: Not built-in. If you need sticky sessions (e.g., in-memory sessions), use an external load balancer (nginx, ALB) with ip_hash or a custom cookie.

newQuestions.question: Explain the Buffer API - alloc, allocUnsafe, from. When is allocUnsafe dangerous?
newQuestions.answer: Buffer.alloc(size): Creates a buffer of size, filled with zeros. Safe. Use when you'll write before reading. Buffer.allocUnsafe(size): Creates a buffer of size without initializing. Contains whatever was in memory (could be old data, secrets). Faster. Dangerous if you read before writing or if the buffer is exposed (e.g., sent over network) before overwriting. Buffer.from(array|string|buffer): Creates a buffer from existing data. Copies the data. Safe. Deprecated: new Buffer() is deprecated due to security (allocUnsafe-like behavior). Use alloc, allocUnsafe, or from. Performance: allocUnsafe is faster for buffers you'll overwrite entirely (e.g., reading from socket into pre-allocated buffer). Otherwise use alloc or from.

newQuestions.question: What is an API Gateway and when would you use one with Node.js?
newQuestions.answer: An API Gateway is a single entry point for client requests. It routes to backend services, handles cross-cutting concerns. Responsibilities: Routing, load balancing, authentication/authorization, rate limiting, request/response transformation, caching, logging. When to use: Microservices—many small services; gateway hides internal structure. Single entry for clients. Centralize auth, rate limiting, etc. instead of in each service. Options: Kong, AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management, nginx. Or a lightweight Node.js gateway (express + routing, or specialized libs). Node.js as gateway: BFF (Backend for Frontend)—Node aggregates multiple backends, tailors response for web/mobile. Good fit: GraphQL gateway, server-side composition.

newQuestions.question: How would you implement structured logging and monitoring in a Node.js app?
newQuestions.answer: Structured logging: Log JSON with fields: timestamp, level, message, requestId, userId, error stack. Use pino or winston. Avoid console.log in production—no structure, slow. Request ID: Generate UUID per request (middleware), attach to req, include in all logs. Enables tracing one request across services. Log levels: error, warn, info, debug. Set level via env. Production: info or warn. Monitoring: Metrics (Prometheus + Grafana): request count, latency percentiles, error rate. Health endpoints for liveness/readiness. APM (e.g., Datadog, New Relic) for traces and performance. Alerts on error spike, latency, saturation. Distributed tracing: OpenTelemetry or Jaeger. Propagate trace IDs across services. Correlate logs with traces.
newQuestions.codeExample: logger.info({ requestId: req.id, userId: req.user?.id }, 'Request completed');
